title: The Thing We Forget When We’re Fed Up
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni offers a short guide to keeping empathy alive when work pressure, competing deadlines and annoying colleagues wear it thin. She opens with a scenario of conflicting data deadlines and then a personal story in which analysts she assumed were incompetent were actually juggling competing priorities and carefully checking details. From there she argues that apparent obstruction is often fear of change, recommending an Emotional Intelligence 2.0 move of acknowledging the other person's feelings before the technical objection. She reminds readers that a green Slack dot hides a whole human life, urging grace and civility, and finishes by reframing empathy as a mindset of pausing and being curious rather than a checkbox.
points: Confusion or delay from a colleague is often a battle of competing priorities, not incompetence, so check assumptions before getting angry.
Repeated roadblocks usually come from fear of change, and asking how the person feels about the change opens the conversation.
Remote colleagues carry unseen stresses behind an active Slack status, so grace and civility cost little and lower the temperature.
Empathy works best as a mindset reached by pausing, breathing and asking instead of assuming, rather than as one more task to tick off.
quotes: The lack of completion and reticence was not incompetence but a battle of competing priorities. He also had one clarifying question before proceeding. It was about grounding the right date format to align. This, too, was not a sign of incompetence but rather of inquisitiveness to make sure things were done right.
But what if the obstacles they are putting up are not necessarily grounded in logic, but primal fear? People hate change, some more than others.
The key here is to bring out the feelings. Get to the root of what they are feeling before tackling the technical aspects. Change is scary, and first, you must face the fear head-on.

When we are emotionally charged, it is easy to forget that a real person is behind the screen. Even in a work environment, it's tempting to be more open with our harsh thoughts and feelings through the keyboard than face to face.

Have grace. Think of the times, with gratitude, someone has had grace for you. Think of how you felt. Do not contribute to the incivility prevalent in the workplace. Be the bringer of calm, a lighter touch, and a general aura of safety.

It is nearly impossible to empathize and be the “bigger person” if you are in a negative state. Breathe. Pause before reacting. Be curious before levying accusation, whether out loud or in your spiraling mind. Calm, then act. Ask, don’t assume.

Your mindset shift by pausing will make it so having empathy or compassion is not just one more task. It is the objective you act on that smooths out the week, relieves the pressure, and brings a bit of calm to the high-velocity work environment.
